site.name: Free Data Broker Removal Guide
site.description: Free people-search opt-out links checked November 10, 2026, the steps that work, and a US state map of who has a legal right to deletion. Official sources. Not legal advice.

broker_removal.disclaimer: Not legal advice. This page is a research guide built from official sources and the sites' own pages, checked on the date shown. It does not apply any law to your situation. For advice, talk to a licensed attorney in your state.

steps.title: Inventory first
steps.detail: List the emails, phone numbers and old accounts you still control. Search each inbox for sign-up and marketing mail to find forgotten accounts.

steps.title: Delete old accounts while you can still sign in
steps.detail: Some sites only accept deletion from a signed-in session. Finish those before you close the email address that gets their codes.

steps.title: Find your listings and confirm they are you
steps.detail: Common names pull up other people. Only opt out of a record that is actually yours.

steps.title: Opt out at the official link, in your own browser
steps.detail: Use the links below. Captchas often fail in automated or remote browsers, so open them yourself.

steps.title: Click verification emails right away
steps.detail: Links commonly expire in 24 hours, and some much sooner. One in our testing expired in about 15 minutes.

steps.title: Save the receipt
steps.detail: Keep the confirmation email or screenshot. Log the result from that message, not from memory. A reply that says denied is easy to misread as done.

steps.title: Recheck later
steps.detail: Look again after the window the site gives (often 3 days), then every month or two. Listings can come back when new public records arrive.

pitfalls: Never pay a people-search site to remove you. Their opt-outs are free.
Delete linked accounts before you delete an old email address.
Where you live matters. Many sites only grant formal privacy rights to residents of states with a comprehensive privacy law. Everyone else gets a courtesy opt-out, if that.
Most state laws exclude publicly available information, such as government records. That is what many listings are built from, so a legal deletion right may not force a takedown.
Do not misstate your state of residence on a form.
If an account-deletion email tells you not to sign back in, don't. Signing in can cancel the deletion on some sites.

broker_removal.arizona: Arizona has no comprehensive consumer privacy law, so Arizona residents have no general legal right to make a people-search site delete a listing. The Arizona Attorney General's consumer pages cover data-breach notice, not deletion, and SB 1815 (2026) was only introduced. Arizona residents can still use each site's free opt-out form. Many sites honor those as a courtesy. Sites that tie formal rights to state law may refuse.
broker_removal.state_limited_note: SmartBackgroundChecks, USPhonebook and FastPeopleSearch publish near-identical privacy notices. They say your privacy rights depend on your state of residence and point residents of states with comprehensive privacy laws to a supplemental notice. They take requests through a web form or by phone. They also say their data is publicly available information, which they consider outside state privacy laws, and that they apply opt-outs to it as a courtesy. If you live in a state without a comprehensive law, such as Arizona, expect a formal privacy request to be refused. The opt-out form is still worth trying.
broker_removal.pai_note: Most comprehensive state privacy laws exclude publicly available information (government records and certain other public data) from 'personal data,' so a deletion right may not reach typical people-search listings.
